articles.title: ‘We’re Crossing a Line Here’ — Former NFL Scout Doesn’t Mince Words on Lane Kiffin Trying to Add NFL Players at LSU
articles.summary: Former Philadelphia Eagles scout John Middlekauff believes the latest NFL-to-college eligibility loophole has pushed college football into uncomfortable terr...
articles.body:
Former Philadelphia Eagles scout John Middlekauff believes the latest NFL-to-college eligibility loophole has pushed college football into uncomfortable territory, even if he does not blame Lane Kiffin for taking advantage of it.

Middlekauff addressed LSU's pursuit of players coming directly from NFL training camps during a recent appearance on Colin Cowherd's podcast, questioning where college football is supposed to draw the line.

John Middlekauff Says NFL-to-College Moves Cross a Line

"Saying that you can go to a training camp and then return to college feels like we're crossing a line here that most people are going to agree upon," Middlekauff said in an Instagram clip . "Like, this is insane."

Middlekauff, who worked in Philadelphia's scouting department before moving into sports media, argued that repeated courtroom losses have steadily weakened the NCAA's ability to enforce a coherent eligibility structure.

"The problem is every time these guys sue, they win," Middlekauff said.

He nevertheless stopped short of blaming Kiffin for LSU's aggressive approach. "I will defend Lane Kiffin here for doing this," Middlekauff said. "These are the rules that he's handed."

He pointed to Tampa Bay Buccaneers edge rusher Jack Pyburn as another example.

Pyburn, a former LSU defender, was among 16 players granted temporary relief in Louisiana that opened a path to another college season. He recorded two sacks in his first NFL preseason game while fighting for a Buccaneers roster spot.

PREDICT THE CFB SEASON: PFN's Free CFB Playoff Predictor

Middlekauff also said an NFL scout told him a top-25 Big Ten program had intentionally kept roster spots available because coaches expected players cut from NFL teams to potentially become eligible again.

That possibility is now running into resistance from the conferences themselves.

SEC Moves To Block Former NFL Players From Returning

The SEC adopted a new policy Tuesday prohibiting players who have been drafted by the NFL, NBA, or WNBA, or listed on rosters in those leagues, from returning to compete at conference schools.

The policy directly threatens LSU's plans for former NFL players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris. Both played for Kiffin at Ole Miss before signing professional contracts this offseason, then angled for moves to LSU after being released.

Wright caught 39 passes for 635 yards and five touchdowns in 2025 while posting an 80.6 PFSN TE Impact grade, which ranked 20th nationally.

The SEC's move puts LSU on notice and gives commissioner Greg Sankey broad authority to enforce the new policy.

The Big Ten adopted its own ban earlier Tuesday. That development addresses the exact concern Middlekauff raised before the conferences acted.

He believes the scenario of NFL training camps serving as a temporary stop before another college season crosses a line. The SEC now appears to agree, even if the courts and the NCAA have not yet settled where that line legally belongs.

articles.title: Is Texas' Cole Hutson still eligible after new SEC eligibility policy?
articles.summary: The SEC has made a stand against players returning to college after being in the pros. How does the new policy impact Texas OL Cole Hutson?
articles.body:
The SEC has joined the Big Ten in preventing former NFL players and other professional athletes from returning to play college sports. The conference announced the new policy Tuesday evening following a meeting of the conference's presidents, chancellors and athletics directors in Birmingham, Alabama.

The new policy was passed unanimously after a 16-0 vote by SEC presidents. The rule's three provisions prohibit former pros from returning to campus. SEC commissioner Greg Sankey has been given the authority to penalize any program that breaks the new rules.

Tuesday's policy announcement from the SEC also comes less than 24 hours after the conference's presidents and chancellors released a statement voicing their opposition to former student-athletes returning to the college ranks after competing professionally.

The SEC announced its institutions are "not permitted" to have an athlete on its roster who has:

Previously declared for the NFL, NBA, or WNBA draft, and did not appropriately withdraw.

Signed a contract with an NFL (or other professional football league), NBA/G-League, or WNBA (or affiliate) team, or ...

Been listed on an NFL (or other professional football league), NBA/G-League, or WNBA (or affiliate) roster."

The rule impacts LSU the most. Lane Kiffin was attempting to add ex-Ole Miss/Browns tight end Dae'Quan Wright and ex-Ole Miss/Saints defensive tackle Xzavian Harris.

But does the new rule impact the return of Texas offensive lineman Cole Hutson ? The short answer is no. Hutson should still be eligible under the new policy. Hutson doesn't technically fit into any of the three categories outlined by the league.

Hutson didn't "declare" for the NFL Draft because he was theoretically out of eligibility. He didn't have to withdraw from the draft because he didn't have to declare. Hutson was not picked in the 2026 NFL Draft. The Austin native was invited to participate in rookie minicamps with the Dallas Cowboys and Cleveland Browns , but he never signed a contract. He didn't join any team as an undrafted free agent and he did not appear on an NFL roster.

That clears Hutson of all three provisions. Obviously, this is a fluid situation and the SEC might move to prohibit players like Hutson that are edge cases. For now, Hutson is still officially on the Texas Longhorns roster .

The lineman was granted a temporary restraining order a few weeks ago by Judge Daniella Deseta Lyttleand. Hutson was scheduled to have another hearing on Aug. 10, also in front of Judge Lyttleand, but that hearing became moot after a group of 2022 athletes filed a class action lawsuit against the NCAA, fighting for extra eligibility for the new academic year while claiming the NCAA violated federal antitrust law.

Judge Charlotte Sweeney of the US District Court of Colorado ultimately ruled in favor of the athletes, finding the harm significant enough to grant the injunction.

"They will suffer irreparable harm without issuance of an injunction. And the balance of equities, as well as the public interest, favor them. They are entitled to the injunctive relief they seek," Sweeney wrote in the decision. "Consistent with the above analysis, the Court grants Plaintiffs' Motion for Temporary Restraining Order, ECF No. 19. DATED this 31st day of July 2026."

After the Colorado ruling, Hutson officially reached an agreement with the NCAA to make him eligible. The lineman was granted one more year.

Hutson, who was part of UT coach Steve Sarkisian's 2022 recruiting class, played in 48 games for Texas before running out of eligibility following the 2025 season.

Even Arch Manning was surprised to see Hutson back on the team.

"I was off social media, so I didn't know what was going on really," Manning said. "And I saw him early morning one day and I was like, 'What the hell?' I gave him a big hug. I'm glad to have him back."

articles.title: SEC and Big Ten Ban Pro Players From Returning to College
articles.summary: The SEC and Big Ten have taken major steps to prevent former professional athletes from returning to college sports after gaining additional eligibility thro...
articles.body:
The SEC and Big Ten have taken major steps to prevent former professional athletes from returning to college sports after gaining additional eligibility through recent legal rulings.

The Big Ten passed a new rule Tuesday preventing football players who have moved into professional football from returning to compete for one of its schools. Under the policy, players who declared for the NFL Draft and did not withdraw, appeared on an NFL roster or signed a professional contract would be prohibited from joining a Big Ten roster.

The SEC followed with an even broader policy covering football and basketball. The conference's rule applies to athletes who have been drafted or appeared on professional rosters, including the NFL, NBA, WNBA and NBA G League. SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey has been given authority to enforce the policy and impose penalties on schools that violate it.

The decisions come amid a major eligibility dispute involving athletes from the 2022 high school class. Recent court rulings have allowed some players to receive additional eligibility and return to college sports after their original eligibility had expired.

The situation has already created controversy around LSU . Head coach Lane Kiffin had been looking to add former NFL players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris after they received additional eligibility through the ongoing legal battle. The SEC's new rule could prevent those players from competing for LSU.

The conferences argue that allowing players who have already entered professional sports to return to college would create an uneven competitive environment. The policies are also designed to maintain a clearer separation between college and professional athletics as eligibility rules continue to change.

However, the issue is far from settled. The new conference rules could face legal challenges as the larger court battle over NCAA eligibility continues. The ACC and Big 12 are also considering similar restrictions, meaning the debate could spread across college athletics in the coming days.

For now, the SEC and Big Ten have made their positions clear: once an athlete has crossed into professional sports, their college career should be over. With lawsuits and eligibility disputes still ongoing, however, this battle is likely to continue well beyond the start of the 2026 season.

articles.title: Rams May Solve Their Third Receiver Question With Rising Pass-Catcher
articles.summary: Rams tight end Terrance Ferguson was a shocking pick in the second round during the 2025 NFL Draft, but he could be set for a breakout. The post Rams May Sol...
articles.body:
Los Angeles Rams tight end Terrance Ferguson was a shocking pick in the second round during the 2025 NFL Draft, and for the most part, he underwhelmed in his rookie year.

He got on the field some during the two- and three-tight-end sets, but he failed to get much going in terms of production.

In 2026, however, things are looking good for Ferguson, as he is healthy and ready to get the season started, with a full season of Sean McVay's system under his belt.

Ferguson is an explosive, vertical tight end who lacks the size and blocking chops to be a true in-line tight end, but he has serious pass-catching and route-running potential.

According to Rams insider Nate Atkins, Ferguson was circled during the offseason as a player who could take a big leap and contribute in his second year.

Now, they are seeing real growth, and he will be their main third option in the passing game.

" Los Angeles opted against adding an obvious third pass catcher behind Puka Nacua and Davante Adams , in part because it has some plans for Ferguson in his second season," Atikins wrote.

"Ferguson had a bumpy start to his rookie year after missing time in training camp with an injury and then waiting half a season to see the field, but he intrigued the Rams by turning his 11 catches into a 21-yard average, and now his route tree is growing beyond simply winning matchups up the seam.

"They are using him on quick passes in matchups with linebackers as well as in alignments at the F (flex), Y (in-line), X (isolated perimeter) and Z (accompanied perimeter) roles.

"He cut weight this offseason to be able to handle all of that, and the challenge will be holding up well enough as a blocker at tight end while doing so. But the path is there for Ferguson to lead a crowded tight end group in catches and yards and to finish third on the team in those categories behind Nacua and Adams."

The Rams rely heavily on Adams and Nacua, both of whom play a physical style that makes them susceptible to injuries.

Nacua especially plays with his helmet down, while Adams is more slick as a route runner, but at his age, he is quite injury-prone

If either of them goes down, Ferguson becomes even more crucial as a key member of the pass attack.

The key thing for him will be how decent a blocker he can be, which can prevent the Rams from tipping their hand about what kind of play they are drawing up.

If Ferguson has lost enough mass, he could also line up on the outside as a receiver.

He is a possible chess piece that can keep the Rams' offense afloat if their top receivers miss time, or if they are healthy, the offense can be the best in the NFL through Ferguson and his versatility.
